newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: FEATURE - Lisbon begins to dismantle "drugs supermarket".
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Lisbon begins to dismantle "drugs supermarket".

text.p: Few of the million tourists who come to delight each year in Lisbon's twisting streets, its quaint trams and colourful 18th century architecture are aware of its existence. Certainly none would visit it.

But clinging to the side of a valley circling the western edge of Portugal's rather delapidated but dignified capital, and out of sight of most visiting eyes, is arguably the worst slum in western Europe.
It is a rabbit warren of ageing housing and illegal, improvised shanty dwellings that has defied city authorities and police for decades.
SLUM BECOMES DRUGS DISTRIBUTION CENTRE

Long used as a refuge by petty criminals, because its narrow lanes and streets are often inaccessible to police vehicles, Casal Ventoso (Windy Village) has in recent years taken on a more sinister and deadly role as Lisbon's "drugs supermarket".
Police calculate it is the distribution centre for a significant amount of the heroin, cocaine and hashish consumed daily on the streets of the capital.
Casal Ventoso has also become a cause celebre for experts in city renewal, who see it as a symbol of years of Portuguese urban neglect and indifference.
"There is really nothing western European about this place," said Paulo de Sousa of the recently-installed office for the development of Casal Ventoso.

Picking his way between dozens of drug addicts openly getting a fix along the so-called "stairway of death" that leads up from the valley floor into the heart of the district, de Sousa waved a rolled up map in the direction of distrusting eyes.
"City surveyors," he said with a cheery, but well-practised smile.

Local officials calculate that Casal Ventoso is home to around 500 addicts by day, with over 100 sleeping rough in its streets at night. A state drugs programme distributes some 3,000 free syringes every day.
DEVELOPMENT PLAN AIMS TO ERADICATE EYESORE
But a $120 million Casal Ventoso development plan, launched with great political fanfare earlier this year, is not really about resolving the drug problem.

Officials admit that, if the dealers were driven out, they would simply set up shop elsewhere, even if it should make the job of the police easier by creating proper access roads into an out of the area.

The purpose is to wipe an eyesore off the map of Lisbon and re-house 4,500 residents, up to 40 percent of whom live in dwellings without running water, in conditions more suitable to Europe at the end of the 20th century, officials say.

"It has been long promised but always postponed," said Cipriano Oliveira, who heads the development project. "We are not aiming to get rid of the drugs but this bairro (district) has become a ghetto," he said.
The $120 million development plan, which will be partly financed by the European Union, calls for the tearing down or renovation of 1,100 dwellings by the turn of the century.
Most residents will be re-housed in new appartment blocks to be built nearby.
SLUM-DWELLERS IGNORED IN RUSH FOR ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT

Local government officials estimate that some 20,000 families live in makeshift housing in and around the Portuguese capital, ignored in the country's rush for economic development since it joined the EU a decade ago.
But few match the degradation of Casal Ventoso.
"If we were talking about building a motorway, this lot would have been knocked down ages ago," de Sousa said.
The degree of social decline is reflected in the fact that some 80 percent of Casal Ventoso children either drop out of school or leave without any type of qualification.
"Life has always been poor, but at least it was humane. Now, all the humanity has gone," said one elderly woman, referring to the drugs invasion.

The development programme began with the symbolic demolishing of eight Casal Ventoso houses in early November, with government ministers and local officials on hand to demonstrate the political significance of the act.
But after all the promises of the past, long-time residents remain sceptical that it will lead to much change. "I will believe it when I see it," said 60-year-old Antonio Augusto.
